cards.body:
Mercy Perry said water came up to his front door and flooded his car, which now will not start, after Saturday's flooding in Indiantown. Perry said the village used to have fairly good drainage and never had this kind of flooding before. Village manager Taryn Kryzda said 6 inches of rain on Saturday simply overwhelmed the drainage system, causing the flooding. Kryzda said the village was finding even in new development that the drainage structures were compromised because of so much rain in a short period of time, and there wasn't one specific area where there were issues.

Perry said he did see village crews out clearing debris from drains on Saturday. Upgrading the drainage infrastructure would take time and money, according to Kryzda. She said the village has already engaged its engineers to start the engineering process, then will create a capital improvement program to prioritize projects and identify funding.

hero.body:
Port St. Lucie homeowners are finding flyers in their mailboxes explaining how the city's $24 million settlement with former trash hauler Waste Pro will appear as credits on their property tax bills. The city sued Waste Pro after two years of unreliable service and missed pickups, and the two sides settled in April for $24 million, days before the case was set to go to trial.

The settlement is being distributed over 95,000 eligible properties. About 57,000 homeowners who have stayed at the same property since the 2022 tax roll will receive an estimated $364 credit. Roughly 38,000 other eligible properties, including newer properties added to the tax roll and those approved through an eligibility claims process, will receive an estimated $64 credit.

The City Council voted in June to return all of the money to residents through property tax credits rather than mailing checks. The decision drew loud objections at the June meeting, with residents telling the council they wanted cash in hand. When the final vote was taken, boos and jeers came from the audience. Only Councilwoman Jolien Caraballo supported mailing checks. Other council members raised concerns about the cost of printing and mailing tens of thousands of checks and the chance that payments could be lost or stolen.

Council members agreed that none of the settlement money would be moved into the city's general fund. Councilman Anthony Bonna said it's the taxpayers' money and the taxpayers were the ones who were wronged. The credits are landing at the same time property owners across St. Lucie County are receiving their TRIM notices, the annual estimate of what they can expect to owe in property taxes. Voters are expected to weigh in on twice-weekly pickup through a straw ballot question in November.
hero.headline: Port St. Lucie homeowners receive notices on Waste Pro settlement credits

cards.body:
Port St. Lucie homeowners are receiving mailed notices explaining how the city's $24 million settlement with former trash hauler Waste Pro will appear as credits on their property tax bills. The settlement, reached in April days before trial, stemmed from the city's lawsuit against Waste Pro after two years of unreliable service and missed pickups. The City Council voted in June to return all the money to residents through property tax credits rather than mailing checks, distributing the settlement over 95,000 eligible properties.

About 57,000 homeowners who stayed at the same property since the 2022 tax roll will receive an estimated $364 credit, while roughly 38,000 other eligible properties, including newer properties and those approved through a claims process, will receive an estimated $64 credit. Deborah Koon-Martin, a Port St. Lucie homeowner, said she thought the settlement would be money, not a credit on her taxes. "You can use the money for other things. You're going to pay your taxes anyway, so it's not really helping," Koon-Martin said.

The June decision to issue credits instead of checks drew loud objections from residents who wanted cash in hand, with boos and jeers from the audience after the final vote. Only Councilwoman Jolien Caraballo supported mailing checks. Other council members raised concerns about the cost of printing and mailing tens of thousands of checks and the chance that payments could be lost or stolen. Councilman Anthony Bonna said none of the settlement money would go into the city's general fund, saying it is the taxpayers' money and the taxpayers were the ones who were wronged.

hero.body:
Indiantown village manager Taryn Kryzda said drainage structures were overwhelmed and compromised after 6 inches of rain on Saturday flooded homes and cars, and the village has now begun a multi-year engineering and capital improvement process to upgrade the infrastructure. Kryzda said the flooding affected multiple areas, including new development where drainage structures failed because of the volume of rain in a short period. Resident Mercy Perry said water came up to his front door and flooded his car, which now will not start.

Kryzda said upgrading the drainage infrastructure will require engineering, a capital improvement program to prioritize projects, and funding identification. The village has already engaged its engineers to start the process. Perry said he saw village crews clearing debris from drains on Saturday.

Perry said Indiantown used to have fairly good drainage and residents never experienced flooding like Saturday's event. More rain fell on Monday, causing residents to watch the sky with worry.

Kryzda said there was not one specific area where drainage issues occurred during Saturday's storm. Perry said the flooding happened suddenly after years without similar problems.

About 57,000 homeowners who have stayed at the same property since the 2022 tax roll will receive an estimated $364 credit, while roughly 38,000 other eligible properties will receive an estimated $64 credit. The credits are landing at the same time property owners across St. Lucie County are receiving their TRIM notices, the annual estimate of what they can expect to owe in property taxes.

The settlement resulted from the city's lawsuit against Waste Pro after two years of unreliable service and missed pickups. The two sides settled in April for $24 million, days before the case was set to go to trial. Council members rejected using settlement money to pay for a second weekly collection day, saying it would only work until the money ran out. hero.body:
Indiantown Village Manager Taryn Kryzda has engaged engineers to begin assessing the drainage system after 6 inches of rain on Saturday overwhelmed the infrastructure and flooded neighborhoods across the community. Kryzda acknowledged that drainage structures were compromised even in new development areas. The engineering work is the first step toward creating a capital improvement program, though the village has not yet identified funding sources for upgrades.

Resident Mercy Perry said water came up to his front door and flooded his car, which now will not start. Perry said the village used to have fairly good drainage and residents never experienced flooding like Saturday's event. Village crews cleared debris from drains on Saturday as the flooding occurred.

Kryzda said the volume of rain in a short period of time caused problems throughout Indiantown rather than in one specific area. Perry said the flooding was sudden and unexpected for the neighborhood.

Kryzda outlined the timeline for drainage improvements, saying the village must first complete engineering work, then create a capital improvement program to prioritize projects, and finally identify funding. On Monday, residents looked at the sky with worry as more rain fell in Indiantown.
hero.headline: Indiantown village manager engages engineers after 6 inches of rain overwhelms drainage system

cards.body:
Willow Lakes LLC, the owner of 203 acres of land off West Midway Road and Interstate 95, submitted a rezoning application in June to St. Lucie County to change 174 acres to light industrial use to allow for a data center. The rezoning application said the applicant intends to develop a data center on the portion of the property to be zoned Light Industrial. The land was originally planned for the Koa Bay Surf Park Community with developer Devcon Enterprises, but those plans fell through after the property owner could not raise sufficient capital for the project.

Attorney Lee Dobbins, who represents Willow Lakes LLC, said the landowner believes the property is well suited for a data center, citing existing Florida Power Light transmission lines on the site and a man-made lake that could be used for a closed-loop cooling system. The rezoning application requests the remaining 26 acres to be zoned general commercial, intended for development for commercial retail uses, and could include a hotel, gas station and restaurants or fast food.

Fort Pierce City Commissioner Michael Broderick said the proposal could be an appropriate use of the land, but he wants developers to demonstrate there will be no impact to groundwater, no impacts to user fees from power consumption and no noise pollution. The application is scheduled to go before the Planning and Zoning Board in September.

hero.body:
Port St. Lucie homeowners are receiving flyers in their mailboxes explaining how the city's $24 million settlement with Waste Pro will appear as credits on their property tax bills. The credits stem from the city's lawsuit against Waste Pro, which Port St. Lucie sued after two years of unreliable service and missed pickups. The two sides settled in April for $24 million, days before the case was set to go to trial.

The settlement is being distributed over 95,000 eligible properties. About 57,000 homeowners who have stayed at the same property since the 2022 tax roll will receive an estimated $364 credit. Roughly 38,000 other eligible properties, including newer properties added to the tax roll and those approved through an eligibility claims process, will receive an estimated $64 credit.

The City Council voted in June to return all of the settlement money to residents through property tax credits rather than mailing checks. The decision drew loud objections at the June meeting, with residents saying they wanted cash in hand. Deborah Koon-Martin, a Port St. Lucie homeowner, said she thought the notice would mean money, not a tax credit. Only Councilwoman Jolien Caraballo supported issuing checks. Other council members raised concerns about the cost of printing and mailing tens of thousands of checks and the chance that payments could be lost or stolen.

The credits are arriving as property owners across St. Lucie County receive their TRIM notices, the annual estimate of what they will owe in property taxes. FCC Environmental Services is the city's current trash hauler. The council considered whether settlement money could pay for a second weekly collection day before rejecting that option, saying it would only work until the money ran out. Voters are expected to weigh in on twice-weekly pickup through a straw ballot question in November.
hero.headline: Port St. Lucie homeowners receive notices about Waste Pro settlement credits on property tax bills

cards.body:
Willow Lakes LLC submitted a rezoning application in June to St. Lucie County to change 174 acres of its 203-acre property off West Midway Road and Interstate 95 to light industrial use to allow for a data center. The land was originally planned for the Koa Bay Surf Park Community with developer Devcon Enterprises, but attorney Lee Dobbins, who represents Willow Lakes LLC, said those plans fell through after the property owner could not raise sufficient capital for the project. The application is scheduled to go before the Planning and Zoning Board in September.

Fort Pierce City Commissioner Michael Broderick said the proposal could be an appropriate use of the land, but he has conditions. Broderick said he wants developers to demonstrate there will be no impact to groundwater, no impacts to user fees from power consumption, and no noise pollution. Broderick said if developers do not meet those conditions, he will not support the proposal.

Parker Whiteside, who lives about a mile and a half from the property, said she values the quiet, open character of the area. When asked about the potential data center, Whiteside said she hates the idea. The rezoning application requests the remaining 26 acres be zoned general commercial for development of commercial retail uses that could include a hotel, gas station, or restaurants.

hero.body:
Port St. Lucie homeowners are finding flyers in their mailboxes explaining how the city's $24 million settlement with its former trash hauler will show up on their property tax bill, not as mailed checks as some residents expected. The credits are the result of the city's lawsuit against Waste Pro, the company Port St. Lucie sued after two years of unreliable service and missed pickups. The two sides settled in April for $24 million, days before the case was set to go to trial. In June, the City Council voted to return all of that money to residents through property tax credits rather than mailing checks.

The settlement is being distributed over 95,000 eligible properties in two tiers. About 57,000 homeowners who have stayed at the same property since the 2022 tax roll would receive an estimated $364 credit. Roughly 38,000 other eligible properties, including newer properties added to the tax roll and those approved through an eligibility claims process, would receive an estimated $64 credit. Deborah Koon-Martin, a Port St. Lucie homeowner, recounted her first reaction to getting the letter. "I thought it was going to be money, not on my taxes," she said.

The decision to issue credits instead of checks drew loud objections at the June meeting. Residents told the council they wanted cash in hand. "You can use the money for other things. You're going to pay your taxes anyway, so it's not really helping," Koon-Martin said. Only Councilwoman Jolien Caraballo supported that approach. Other council members raised concerns about the cost of printing and mailing tens of thousands of checks and the chance that payments could be lost or stolen. When the final vote was taken, boos and jeers came from the audience.

The credits are landing at the same time property owners across St. Lucie County are receiving their TRIM notices, the annual estimate of what they can expect to owe in property taxes. The city's current trash hauler is FCC Environmental Services. Residents have continued pressing the city over once-a-week pickup, and the council considered whether settlement money could pay for a second weekly collection day before rejecting that option, saying it would only work until the money ran out. Voters are expected to weigh in on twice-weekly pickup through a straw ballot question in November.

Broderick said if developers do not meet those conditions, he will not be supportive of the project.

Parker Whiteside, who lives about a mile and a half from the property, said she values the quiet, open character of the area and opposes the data center.
